name: England
summary_text: England stands under the United Kingdom's national framework. Passport and document rules, entry and visa rules, marriage law and criminal law are uniform across the country, and the single-sex-services regime operates through the national equality legislation and the national equality watchdog, with no devolved layer between a visitor and those institutions. The United Kingdom Supreme Court sits in London and the Equality and Human Rights Commission's headquarters are in England, so the machinery that governs a trans visitor's day here is the machinery of the whole state.  The defining judgment is the unanimous ruling of the United Kingdom Supreme Court in For Women Scotland, handed down on 16 April 2025. The court held that "woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological woman and biological sex, and that a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. Those definitions govern services, searches and detention allocation in England.  The Equality and Human Rights Commission, the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales, updated its code of practice after the Supreme Court ruling. As reported on 20 May 2025, the code advises that services and businesses may ask a person for their birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety. This is the operative guidance a trans visitor meets at venues, on transport and in services from day to day.  Prison and custody allocation follows the same principle. On 19 June 2026 Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down Scottish Prison Service guidance that had allowed some trans prisoners to be housed according to gender identity, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis in line with the April 2025 definition-of-a-woman ruling. The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment. A judicial review reported on 5 February 2026 tested how far the April 2025 ruling reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide: government lawyers argued that a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy "Orwellian".  The Home Office's England-and-Wales hate-crime statistics, published 9 October 2025, record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025. The transgender strand fell 11% and the sexual-orientation strand fell 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence, with the Crime Survey estimating about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year, and that a February 2024 Metropolitan Police recording-system change means earlier years over-counted. These are the official baseline figures for trans-hostile incidents in the jurisdiction where the national framework applies directly.

sources.title: Goodwin v United Kingdom (2002) - European Court of Human Rights
sources.documents: Found UK in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights under Corbett status quo; ruling led to passing of Gender Recognition Act 2004.
sources.detail: Cited as 2002 European Court of Human Rights case Goodwin v United Kingdom, breach of Articles 8 and 12

sources.title: ILGA-Europe Review of LGBTI Rights - 2015, 2020, 2025 reports
sources.documents: Institutional human-rights ranking documenting backsliding: UK highest score in Europe in 2015 with 86% (92% Scotland), 9th place 66% in 2020 with concern about 'hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups', 22nd place 45% in 2025, third steepest drop.
sources.detail: Cited as ILGA-Europe's 2015 review, 2020 ranking, and 2025 report

sources.title: Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013
sources.documents: Allows same-sex marriage in England and Wales, with full rights of civil marriage; no religious body compelled; Church of England and Church in Wales explicitly banned.
sources.detail: Passed July 2013, came into force 13 March 2014, first marriages 29 March 2014

sources.title: Civil Partnership Act 2004

sources.detail: Passed 18 November 2004, came into effect 5 December 2005
